brief.goal: Understand how a green leaf makes its own food from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide

big_idea.text: A green leaf uses sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to make glucose food and release oxygen; this food-making process is photosynthesis.

why_it_matters.text: The glucose plants make feeds their own growth and supports food chains, while photosynthesis also adds oxygen to the air.

the_why.text: A leaf can build glucose only when all its needed inputs arrive: water comes up from the roots, carbon dioxide enters from the air, and chlorophyll captures sunlight. If carbon dioxide is removed, the leaf cannot make starch food, even in sunlight.

objectives.can: Name the materials a green leaf needs and the products it makes during photosynthesis.
Explain why a green leaf without carbon dioxide cannot make its food even when it has sunlight and water.
Predict whether a leaf will make food when one required condition is missing.
Use the word equation to describe how a leaf makes food.

picture.text: Start with one broad green leaf attached to a plant. Draw a blue arrow carrying water from the roots up the stem, a grey arrow carrying carbon dioxide from air through tiny leaf pores, and yellow sunlight arrows into the green leaf; then transform the arrows inside the leaf into a glucose-food box and an oxygen arrow leaving the leaf. Finally, write the word equation beneath the same leaf.
picture.standard: Photosynthesis input-output diagram: carbon dioxide and water enter a green leaf

card.diagram_ask: Labelled photosynthesis input-output diagram of one green leaf on a plant: yellow sunlight arrows into the leaf, blue water arrow travelling from roots up the stem, grey carbon-dioxide arrow entering through a labelled stoma, a glucose-food box inside the leaf, and an oxygen arrow leaving the leaf.

needs_first.text: Recognise that plants have roots, stems, and green leaves.
Know that sunlight is light from the Sun and that water and air are around plants.

mistakes.mistake: “Sunlight and water are enough for a green leaf to make food.”
mistakes.why_it_fails: A leaf also needs carbon dioxide from the air; the part kept without carbon dioxide did not show starch after the test.

mistakes.mistake: “Every part of a leaf makes food equally well.”
mistakes.why_it_fails: In a leaf with green and non-green patches, starch was detected in the green patches exposed to light, showing that chlorophyll is needed.

mistakes.mistake: “Plants only take in gases; they do not release oxygen.”
mistakes.why_it_fails: Photosynthesis releases oxygen, and leaf pores exchange carbon dioxide and oxygen.

mistakes.mistake: “Food made by a plant stays only in its leaves.”
mistakes.why_it_fails: Food made mainly in leaves can be carried to other parts of the plant and stored there.

opening_question.question: A green leaf has sunlight and water, but no carbon dioxide from the air. Do you think it can still make its food?
guesses: Yes, because sunlight gives the plant its food.
Yes, because water and sunlight are enough.
No, because the leaf needs something from the air too.
opening_question.answer: No. It cannot make food without carbon dioxide, even if sunlight, water, and a green leaf are present.

route.what: Show one green leaf with a sun and a blue water arrow, but block the grey air arrow. Ask whether this leaf can still make food.
Pause for the learner to choose: sunlight and water are enough, or the leaf also needs a gas from air.
Uncover the grey carbon-dioxide arrow entering a tiny pore on the leaf, and trace the blue water arrow from roots up to the leaf.

Place two halves of the same leaf side by side: one half has carbon dioxide and one does not. Ask which half can make starch, then reveal food only on the carbon-dioxide side because that gas is an essential ingredient.
Circle sunlight, water, carbon dioxide, and chlorophyll on the same leaf picture; name the process photosynthesis and add glucose food plus oxygen as outputs.
Build the word equation beneath the leaf, moving carbon dioxide and water across an arrow labelled sunlight and chlorophyll to glucose and oxygen.
Show green and non-green patches of one sunlit leaf side by side. Ask which patch makes detectable starch, then show that the green patch has chlorophyll to capture sunlight.
Present a leaf with water, chlorophyll, and sunlight but no carbon dioxide. Ask the learner to decide whether glucose and oxygen will be made and explain why.
The learner completes a short paper challenge by testing four leaf-condition cards against the required inputs.
The learner says the word equation in ordinary words: a green leaf uses sunlight to turn water and carbon dioxide into glucose food and oxygen.

questions.question: One half of a green leaf is in sunlight and has water, but carbon dioxide is removed from the air around it. What will happen in that half?
options: It will not make starch food.
It will make starch because sunlight and water are enough.
It will make extra starch because no air can get in.
questions.explain: It cannot make food because carbon dioxide is one of the required materials for photosynthesis.

questions.question: Which set shows everything a green leaf needs to make food?
options: Sunlight, water, carbon dioxide, and chlorophyll.
questions.explain: Chlorophyll captures sunlight, while water and carbon dioxide are changed into glucose; oxygen is released rather than used as a photosynthesis input.

questions.question: Which word equation matches the arrows in the leaf picture?
options: Carbon dioxide + water —with sunlight and chlorophyll→ glucose + oxygen.
Oxygen + water —with sunlight→ carbon dioxide + glucose.
Glucose + carbon dioxide —with sunlight→ water + oxygen.
questions.explain: The leaf takes in carbon dioxide and water, then uses captured sunlight to make glucose and release oxygen.

try_it.title: Leaf ingredient check
try_it.stands_for: Each drawn leaf is a food factory; each tick means that required ingredient reaches that leaf.
try_it.predict: Before you tick anything, predict: can a leaf with sunlight, water, and chlorophyll but without carbon dioxide make food?
steps: Draw four small green leaves and label them A, B, C, and D.
Write these ingredients beside each: A has all four; B has no sunlight; C has no carbon dioxide; D has no chlorophyll.
Circle every leaf that you predict can make glucose food.
Write “no food” beside each leaf missing an ingredient.
Check your choices using the word equation.
try_it.observe: Only leaf A, the leaf with sunlight, water, carbon dioxide, and chlorophyll, can make food.
try_it.question: Why do leaves B, C, and D fail to make food?
try_it.expected: Each fails because photosynthesis needs all four conditions: sunlight, water, carbon dioxide, and chlorophyll. Removing even one means the leaf cannot make glucose.
try_it.write:
“A green leaf makes food when it has ______, ______, ______, and ______.”
“Leaf ___ cannot make food because it lacks ______.”
try_it.in_class: Pairs complete the four-leaf grid for three minutes. The teacher writes “sunlight + water + carbon dioxide + chlorophyll → glucose + oxygen” and the four leaf conditions on the board. Ask, “Which leaves make food, and what missing ingredient stops each other leaf?” If many pairs select a leaf without carbon dioxide, they are treating sunlight and water as sufficient.

leave_out: The detailed light-dependent reactions, Calvin cycle, ATP, NADPH, thylakoids, and stroma.
C3, C4, and CAM pathways and desert-plant adaptations.
The balanced chemical-symbol equation and its numerical coefficients.
Plant respiration, xylem and phloem transport, except for the simple water-to-leaf arrow needed in this picture.

from_lectures.took: The clear whole-plant route: roots supply water, stomata admit carbon dioxide, chlorophyll captures light, and glucose plus oxygen result.
from_lectures.left: The two reaction stages, C3/C4/CAM categories, and rate factors, because they exceed the foundation goal for this short lesson.

from_lectures.took: The emphasis that photosynthesis makes glucose and releases oxygen, plus the useful correction that plants also respire.
from_lectures.left: Chloroplast compartments, reaction stages, and CAM adaptation, because the learner first needs the visible input-output model.

from_lectures.took: The useful tracing of water from roots and gases through stomata before naming the overall process.
from_lectures.left: Electron transport, photosystems, proton gradients, and Calvin-cycle chemistry, because these mechanisms are not needed to explain the Class 7 word equation.

uncited: Recognise that plants have roots, stems, and green leaves.
Know that sunlight is light from the Sun and that water and air are around plants.
The paper-grid task format, its classroom timing, and its diagnostic interpretation are instructional design choices.
